items.title: In a story about rising Chinese consumption Xinhua notes that in the first three quarters of 2026, "domestic consumption contributed nearly half of ec...
items.description_html:
In a story about rising Chinese consumption Xinhua notes that in the first three quarters of 2026, "domestic consumption contributed nearly half of economic growth, driving GDP growth up by 2.1 percentage points".

What it doesn't say is that excluding twice during the COVID years, the only time China has posted a lower consumption contribution to GDP growth year was in 2024, when consumption contributed 44.9% of GDP growth, just a little less than the 46.7% if has contributed so far this year.

On the other hand in the last ten years, consumption has contributed on average 51.3% of GDP growth, and last year it contributed 52.0% of GDP growth, both of which are still well below the global average of 75%.

Rather than suggest that consumption is recovering in 2026, in other words, it would be more correct for Xinhua to suggest that it is lagging more than ever.

items.description_html:
RT Ananth Rupanagudi
200 year old Haveli of Seth Dewan Amarnath— Eminabad Distt Gujranwala, Punjab, Pakistan. Seth Dewan Amarnath was a highly influential figure in undivided India, best known for his magnificent, centuries-old family mansion, the Haveli of Seth Dewan Amarnath, located in the historic town of Eminabad in the Gujranwala District of Punjab, Pakistan.

Belonging to the prominent Hindu Chopra family of Eminabad, Dewan Amarnath Chopra served as the Prime Minister of the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir during the early 1900s. He was a major landowner, holding over 10,000 acres in Gujranwala and adjoining districts alongside a royal jagir (land grant) in Kashmir. He was widely celebrated for his philanthropy, establishing educational institutions, medical dispensaries, and hostels in the region.

Following the Partition of British India in 1947, the Chopra family migrated to India, leaving behind their ancestral estate, which was subsequently used to house incoming refugees for decades before parts of it were repurposed into a school.

Built originally during the era of the Sikh Empire, the structure seamlessly blended Mughal, Sikh, and British colonial architectural influences. It was renowned for its intricate Punjabi craftsmanship, featuring grand arched entryways, beautifully detailed jharokhas (balconies), and vibrant, glowing wall frescoes.

In its prime, the monumental four-storey haveli was an absolute behemoth, encompassing between 100 to 120 rooms. Today, the property is in a critical state of neglect and decay. To prevent catastrophic collapses, two of its upper storeys were previously taken down after a heavy structural railing failed. The remnants—most famously its massive carved entrance door—are gradually crumbling or being replaced by modern concrete buildings. #Punjab #Partition #legacy

As India advances towards the more ambitious and hard-to-attain 500 GW non-fossil domestic target by 2030, the central challenge is no longer merely the scale of non-fossil capacity deployment. Rather, it lies in ensuring that this capacity is effectively integrated into the power system and translated into actual clean electricity generation that delivers broad socioeconomic benefits. India’s rise is often measured in GDP, infrastructure & global influence. But one number deserves far more attention: 496 million.

According to the World Bank’s October 2026 brief
-Nearly 50 cr Indians moved above the $4.20/day lower-middle-income poverty line between 2011 and 2023.
-Share of Indians below this threshold fell from 58% to 16% while extreme poverty dropped from 27.1% to 2.6%.
- Rising employment, greater participation of rural women in paid work, higher consumption & expanded social protection have all contributed
-Challenges like inequality and economic vulnerability remain. But this is a remarkable transformation for a country of India’s scale.

India’s rise isn’t just about a bigger economy but It’s about millions of people gaining a better economic future. This is progress that matters. 🇮🇳

CareEdge Ratings’ latest BFSI analysis points to a cooling in banking system momentum as quarter-end gains unwound. While credit and deposit growth remain robust on a year-on-year basis, liquidity dynamics and funding costs warrant close monitoring.

Key takeaways:
• Bank credit growth eased to 18.2% YoY from 19.4% at September-end, following a post quarter-end decline in outstanding credit.
• Deposit growth moderated to 16.7% YoY, with the credit-deposit growth gap largely unchanged at 151 bps.
• The loan-to-deposit ratio rose to 81.6%, marking its third consecutive increase, indicating persistent funding pressures.
• The WACR climbed above the repo rate as surplus liquidity narrowed, signalling firmer money market conditions.
• CD issuance declined, but wholesale funding costs could remain under pressure as liquidity conditions tighten.

India’s credit card spending declined 5.9% y-o-y to Rs 2.04 lakh crore in September 2026, marking the first annual decline since February 2021. However, the fall was largely influenced by a high base and the shift of festive sales from September last year to October this year.

Key takeaways:
• Card spending fell despite a 10.5% y-o-y rise in cards outstanding, indicating slower spend intensity.
• Transactions surged 23.2% y-o-y, while average ticket size dropped 23.6%, reflecting increased usage for smaller-value payments.
• Online spending declined 12.5% y-o-y, whereas PoS spending grew 7.2%, leading to a lower online share of total spends.
• Private banks strengthened their spending share, while spending growth outside major issuers remained mixed.

Nepal’s edible oil refining industry has grown into a major export-oriented sector, but its fortunes remain closely tied to tariff differentials and policy decisions across borders. A key takeaway from our latest analysis: tariff arbitrage continues to be the primary driver of export competitiveness, making the sector highly sensitive to regulatory shifts.

Key insights:
• Recent duty reductions by India have narrowed the tariff advantage enjoyed by Nepalese refiners, potentially moderating export growth and profitability.
• Strong earnings in FY25-FY26 were supported by favourable tariff arbitrage, but margin pressures may re-emerge as the duty gap contracts.
• Inventory holding risks remain significant, particularly in a volatile commodity price environment.
• Debt servicing metrics, liquidity, and leverage will remain vulnerable if profitability weakens over a prolonged period.
• Going forward, India's import duty regime and global edible oil price movements will be critical variables to watch.

CareEdge-ESG analyses why the answer matters for India’s industrial strategy.
With the EU’s CBAM now in its definitive phase, carbon intensity is increasingly shaping market access and cost structures for steel, aluminium, fertilisers and hydrogen. For India, green hydrogen is emerging as a strategic industrial question, even as the economics remain challenging.

Key takeaways from our latest analysis:

Green hydrogen production costs in India remain 2–2.5x higher than grey hydrogen, making cost parity the sector’s biggest hurdle.

The global market faces a significant execution challenge, with projects that are operational, under construction or near FID far below announced pipelines for 2030.

For Indian steel exporters, CBAM-related carbon costs could materially influence competitiveness, strengthening the case for low-carbon production pathways.

India’s combination of policy support, low-cost renewable energy and large industrial demand creates a meaningful opportunity, provided execution keeps pace with ambition.

Private investment of $180–200 billion is expected through 2030, though announced commitments still exceed FID-backed investment.

The real question for ESG-oriented investors and industrial strategists is where value will concentrate across the value chain.

Q2FY27 highlights an interesting divergence beneath the headline numbers. While credit growth remained robust, the improvement in sector-wide margins was largely driven by PSBs, even as funding costs continued to weigh on larger private banks.

Key insights:
• SCBs’ credit growth accelerated to 20.8% y-o-y, supported by corporate, MSME and retail lending demand.
• Deposit growth improved to 16.2% y-o-y, narrowing the credit-deposit growth gap and easing funding pressures.
• Sector-wide NIM rose to 2.98%, with PSBs posting a stronger improvement, while PVB margins remained flat amid FCNR(B)-related funding cost pressures.
• With repo-linked loans repricing faster than deposits, margins are expected to remain broadly stable with an upward bias in H2FY27.

The next phase of banking performance may be determined less by credit growth and more by the ability to sustain funding efficiency.

France's (A+/Negative) fiscal and debt metrics remain under pressure, as fiscal slippages have kept the debt trajectory elevated. With public debt continuing to exceed medium-term targets and recent budget measures offering only a modest reduction in the fiscal deficit, investor concerns have intensified amid rising debt-servicing costs, weak growth prospects and expectations of continued debt accumulation.

RT Gregg Carlstrom
A few takeaways from a gloomy @IISS_org Manama Dialogue this weekend:

- Very real sense of dread about another, more destructive round of war in the coming weeks, which is unsurprising

- Gulf states are clear and unanimous that they don't want it, a difference from February, when messages to Washington were rather more mixed

- At the same time, there was a feeling of resignation: no one willing to criticize the Trump administration in public, nor to talk in private about what sort of pressure they might bring to bear on America

- There were even some bizarro-world discussions about opportunities for growth and connectivity in the Gulf. Trump is driving a car with no brakes, Gulf states are strapped on the roof, and people are somehow still talking about, like, IMEC and data centers

- Barely any American representation, at a moment when America is deciding the fate of its Gulf allies

- No clarity on what sort of deal (sequencing, nuclear concessions, etc.) the Trump administration would actually be willing to accept. And a broad consensus that Trump himself may not be clear

- Lots of upbeat talk about the Mecca pact, middle powers playing a role in maritime security and so on; little evidence any of this is making a difference yet

- Gargash offered some well-founded criticism of Gulf states failing to work together this year; everyone else offered paeans to Gulf solidarity that seem disconnected from reality

In general, the feeling was a world in torpor: nobody wants this, and nobody has any great ideas for how to stop it

items.description_html:
RT Basha باشا
Speaking at the 22nd @IISS_org Manama Dialogue #IISS_MD26, Dr. Anwar Gargash @AnwarGargash, Diplomatic Adviser to the UAE President @MohamedBinZayed, warned that the Gulf remains trapped in a prolonged state of “no war, no peace,” with Washington and Tehran still far apart. “If these positions are not bridged, then we have to worry about the worst,” he said. Gargash stressed that the UAE opposes another round of confrontation and supports diplomatic efforts, including Qatar’s mediation, but remains “braced for the worst” and prepared to defend its sovereignty, citizens, and economic infrastructure.

On Bahrain and Saudi Arabia, Gargash praised Bahrain’s resilience under Iranian attacks, saying the Kingdom had shown “steadfastness,” “courage,” and the ability to protect its population. He expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia following attacks on civilian airports and infrastructure, declaring, “Nobody can in any way justify an attack on civilian airports and civilian infrastructure.” He emphasized that Gulf security is interconnected and that threats to Bahrain or Saudi Arabia directly affect the UAE and other GCC states.

On the GCC’s collective response, Gargash delivered one of his strongest assessments, acknowledging that Gulf states had failed to respond effectively as a bloc. “We have not collectively risen to the challenge,” he said. While individual countries had demonstrated resilience, he warned that confidence in the GCC’s collective ability to confront a crisis of this magnitude “has in many cases proven to be hollow, unfortunately.” He called for “rebuilding Gulf confidence,” acknowledging that the process would take many years.

On Iran, Gargash distinguished between restoring diplomatic relations and rebuilding trust. “What really has been broken is the confidence,” he said, stressing that it had been shattered by Iran’s attacks on Gulf countries. While Iran remains an essential neighbor and diplomatic and economic relations will eventually resume, rebuilding trust would take “an extremely long time.”

On the Strait of Hormuz, Gargash described restoring the prewar status quo as “important and non-negotiable.” He rejected restrictions on energy exports and international trade, arguing that Gulf countries should not bear the economic consequences of “a crisis that we did not create.”

On relations with Washington, Gargash reaffirmed the importance of the UAE’s security partnership with the United States, saying the crisis had “concretized that relationship” and made it “even more important.” He stressed that American cooperation remains central to the UAE’s security calculations, alongside its own political will and military air defense capabilities.

Gargash also questioned the effectiveness of regional middle powers, arguing that diplomatic conferences and mediation initiatives had failed to produce meaningful results in a crisis fundamentally driven by Washington and Tehran.

He concluded that the UAE continues to seek a political settlement and does not believe a military solution is viable. However, he cautioned that avoiding renewed confrontation cannot be guaranteed if diplomatic efforts fail to bridge the divide between the United States and Iran.

items.description_html:
The global copper market is extremely tight:

China's copper import premium over London Metal Exchange (LME) prices has surpassed $200 per ton, the largest premium on record.

The Yangshan premium, named after a Shanghai port that serves as a major hub for Chinese copper imports, has more than doubled over the last 3 months.

Since the beginning of 2026, this figure has surged +700%.

Furthermore, the premium of spot prices over three-month futures on the LME widened to $217 per ton, the largest since mid-August.

This has been driven by strong Chinese copper demand and domestic inventories falling below typical seasonal levels.

At the same time, expectations of potential US tariffs on refined copper have redirected hundreds of thousands of tons of copper to the US, leaving global inventories heavily concentrated in the country.

The physical copper supply squeeze is far from over.

items.title: RT Digant Haria: Muthoot Finance Q2 - When rising NPAs do not signal bad news For lending companies, the most dreaded acronym is NPA. Rising NPAs gene...
items.description_html:
RT Digant Haria
Muthoot Finance Q2 - When rising NPAs do not signal bad news

For lending companies, the most dreaded acronym is NPA. Rising NPAs generally imply lower future growth & profits. The only exception to this is gold loans due to the technicalities involved in the product. Let's understand this from what happened in Muthoot Finance's Q2 results - NPAs increased sharply, almost doubling in just one quarter.

Why did the NPAs increase?
Prior to 1st April 2026, Muthoot used to offer 12 month bullet repayment loans. Thus, an account would become NPA only if the customer doesn't pay anything for 15 months.

In order to comply with new RBI guidelines on LTVs, most gold loan NBFCs including Muthoot launched new products such as monthly repayment loans, 3 month bullet repayment loans, 6 month bullet repayment loans from 1st April 2026. These loans can become NPA in the 4th, 7th, 10th month respectively if the customer doesn't pay regularly (which is the case with most NBFC type customers).

The current increase in NPAs for Muthoot Finance are a result of the above changes. Comparing today's NPA with previous years is a meaningless exercise, because most current NPAs are technical in nature (and do not signify a 15 month delay in repayment). In all likelihood, the NPAs will increase further in the coming quarters as the new products season.

Do these NPAs impact Muthoot's profits?
NPAs are a problem only if they lead to losses in future. In case of Muthoot, they mentioned in the concall that the LTV on their Stage 2 and Stage 3 portfolio is less than 68%, which means that the value of the gold it holds against these loans is 50% higher than the outstanding dues. Thus, the potential of loss on these loans is extremely low.

Surely, there is a near term impact in terms of interest income reversal and provisioning. But that will get reversed in the subsequent quarters when the customers come and repay their loans. The analyst and investor community may take some time to come to terms with this new reality of the gold loan business -- optically high NPAs, but no meaningful impact on long term profitability.

Q2 performance (beyond NPA)
Muthoot Finance's quarterly performance was characterised by strong loan growth, decent tonnage growth, good improvement in lending yields, and sharp rebound in profitability. Beyond the numbers, this quarterly performance also put an end to some negative narratives that are prevalent in the market

Narrative: Muthoot is the biggest loser in this hypercompetitive market
Fact: Muthoot has not only grown its tonnage & loan growth, but has also been able to improve its lending yields.

Narrative: Muthoot will report zero profit growth in FY27
Fact: Despite the high base of FY26, Muthoot has been able to grow its profits in high double digits. It seems to be on track to report 15%+ growth in profits for FY27 vs. analyst expectation of 0%.

It is an ideal set-up for negativity to end and positivity to start. Muthoot is India's largest gold loan NBFC and its share price has corrected by ~40% since Feb26 despite delivering three good quarters in a row. It is trading at 1.9x on FY27 book (30% discount to long term average) despite growing at 20%+ and reporting best-in-India RoEs of 25%+

Due to its long history, Muthoot Finance navigated through multiple regulatory & gold price cycles. Thanks to its relentless focus on gold appraisal and deep customer connect, it has always managed to come out with negligible credit losses. There is no reason to believe that things will not be the same in this cycle. The only risk is if gold prices crack another 15-20% from current oversold levels of $3900.

Note: 100% of this has been written by human intelligence

items.description_html:
RT Rishabh Karnawat
Many of you don't understand how serious this is, so let me break it down.

In computer science there is a famous kind of puzzle called 3-SAT. You are given a long list of yes-or-no switches and a set of rules about how they must be arranged, and you have to find a combination that satisfies every rule. The obvious way to solve it is to try every combination, but each new switch doubles the number of possibilities, so a puzzle with a few hundred switches would take longer than the age of the universe to brute force.

For decades, the smartest people in the field found clever tricks that made this a little faster, but every trick still hit the same wall: the time required kept exploding as the puzzle grew.
About 25 years ago, two computer scientists, Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi, working with Francis Zane, turned that wall into a formal idea.

They proposed the Exponential Time Hypothesis, which says this explosion is not a failure of human cleverness but a law of nature. No algorithm, however brilliant, will ever solve 3-SAT without the time blowing up exponentially. Nobody could prove it, but almost everyone believed it, and it became one of the foundations of modern computer science.

Researchers used it as a measuring stick. If you could show that solving some other problem quickly would also crack 3-SAT quickly, you had shown that problem was hopelessly hard too. Hundreds of papers, across scheduling, graphs, logic and much more, rest on this one assumption.

Now an internal AI model at OpenAI claims to have broken it. It says it found an algorithm that solves these puzzles meaningfully faster than the hypothesis allows, and it has checked the proof in a computer verification system called Lean.

And here is the remarkable part: the very people who proposed the hypothesis, Impagliazzo and Paturi, along with MIT's Ryan Williams, are now leading the public review of whether a machine has disproved their own idea.
So what happens next? If the disproof holds, a large part of theoretical computer science has to be revisited.

Every result that said "this problem cannot be solved faster, assuming ETH" loses its foundation, and researchers will have to work out which of those walls were real and which were simply where we stopped looking. It does not mean everything becomes easy. The new algorithm is still slow in absolute terms and this is not the famous P versus NP problem being solved.

But it means our map of what is possible was wrong in a place we were very confident about, and it was an AI that redrew it. If the disproof fails, the hypothesis survives and the field breathes out, but we will still have watched an AI produce serious, checkable work on one of the deepest questions in the discipline, closely enough that the founders of the idea had to take it seriously. Either way, something has shifted.

3. When will it take effect? : Effective December 1, 2026

Less paperwork for foreign investors.
Fewer repetitive compliance requirements.
Lower administrative costs.
Easier to do business in Indian markets.
A step towards making India more investor-friendly.

SEBI is trying to make life easier for FPIs and reduce compliance hurdles to encourage foreign investment into Indian markets.

In simple terms: Less paperwork, fewer KYC checks and easier compliance for foreign investors.

Aerospace , Pharma , Metals , Chemicals lot of these sectors require global customer mapping , for us to realize the true depth of capability , competitive environment, profit pool mapping and where they stand, we need to know what is the situation at the customer end

The type of customers will make it easy to determine the growth you will see here , if in a pharma company the customer is top 10 pharma with heavy skew in phase 3 molecules in a particular therapy such as ADC/peptides then you map out who in the world has done the capex in that in India , most of them you cant find directly on relationships as they have NDA's but you will easily get a broad idea , and then map out the commercial performance of that molecule to see if the Indian player is a preferred supplier or in a category of suppliers , then you can quantify the kind of growth Metals + Chemicals = China , the giant in the room , capacities + pricing + regulation , all 3 determine industry profit pools

Aerospace: tier wise capability mapping that enables the company to participate with OEM's at a relationship level rather than a supplier level , if they have that depth and time they can deliver to the customer , it is a very difficult business to be in if you are a tier 1 player but also rewarding in the duopoly of commercial

These are some of the starting points that later become obvious when studying a business and now valuing them from aspects is another aspect that is more important , but must be remembered , otherwise you can follow Value Equity😃

items.description_html:
Always Stay Diversified! ⚠️

Ideally, maintain a portfolio of at least 20-25 stocks

Because in markets, one press release can change the entire story overnight

You can do all the research, track every quarter & still get hit by a risk you never saw coming

Risks can emerge from absolutely anywhere:
- Corporate governance issues
- Geopolitical developments
- Regulatory changes
- Business disruptions
- Income tax raids & investigations
- Unexpected tax liabilities
- Management misconduct or fraud
- Legal disputes
- Cybersecurity breaches

The list is endless

We have witnessed far too many such accidents in the markets lately

No matter how strong your conviction is, never allow one stock to decide the fate of your entire portfolio

Diversification won't eliminate risk, but it can prevent a single mistake or unexpected event from derailing your entire portfolio

It is about surviving the risks you cannot predict

For God's sake, take this seriously

One bad event should hurt your portfolio, not destroy it

**Survival comes first. Compounding follows.**

In 2004, India’s official count said the Sariska Tiger Reserve in Rajasthan had 16-18 tigers. But, visitors had not seen one in months.

This is the story of how a country that has learnt to lived with tigers for millennia, learnt again how to protect it.

items.description_html:
RT Madison Mills
SCOOP: Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents inside customer accounts, including some attempting to take actions that appear to be independent of user instructions, sources told Axios.

The findings have alarmed banking executives, who are racing to restrict access to their systems as AI moves at a velocity faster than financial institutions can respond, multiple industry and bank executives told Axios.

Several banks are now preparing for worst-case and even “day after” scenarios, including how to rapidly secure or restore customer accounts if things go wrong, the people said.

Several bank executives told Axios they're struggling to distinguish between human users and AI agents. One executive said banks also struggle to determine whether agents are authorized by customers or potentially operating without their permission, more akin to rogue agent behavior.

America Has Oil. So Why Is Its Top Diplomat Flying to a Refinery in Gujarat?

That's the surprise in the global energy crisis.

🇺🇸 US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is heading to Reliance's Jamnagar refinery.

His agenda? Get Reliance to refine more Venezuelan crude and explore oil production in Venezuela.

Now connect this with Morgan Stanley's latest research.

The global oil bottleneck is shifting from crude availability to refining capacity, particularly diesel.

🇳🇱 Netherlands: Imports crude, exports refined fuels.

🇮🇳 India: Imports nearly 90% of its crude, yet exports diesel.

🇪🇺 Europe: Remains structurally dependent on imported diesel.

The irony? America is looking to an Indian refinery to help address global energy security.

And here lies India's opportunity.

Higher crude prices can hurt our economy, while stronger diesel refining margins could benefit companies like Reliance.

Oil reserves create geopolitical power. Refining capacity may increasingly determine who captures the profits.

Rubio's Jamnagar visit is more than diplomacy. It's a reminder of how strategically important India's refining industry has become.

items.description_html:
RT Pratik Bhakta
After payments and travel, Juspay’s next big bet is building an open-source competitor to Slack and Jira.

The SoftBank-backed startup is building Xyne.

It is an open-source software platform which can bring an enterprise-knowledge base into a singular AI-powered engine helping large companies build powerful tools for internal actions.

Its second payments bet is on international expansion. If Juspay has managed to solve merchant checkout problems in India, can it do the same for the other major economies too?

It has been trying international markets for a few years now, but the chockey stick curve is finally here, Juspay believes.

These bold bets have come at a huge cost, Juspay has swung from profits into net losses.

But Sheetal Lalwani of Juspay believes he is not burning marketing dollars, he is placing an outsized bet on the future.
